title: Sarde a Beccafico
subtitle: Sicilian stuffed sardines baked in breadcrumbs and pine nuts
excerpt: Sarde a beccafico are butterflied fresh sardines filled with a sweet-and-savoury stuffing of breadcrumbs, pine nuts, raisins, and orange, rolled up and baked with bay leaves between them. A flagship dish of Palermo. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Sarde a beccafico is one of the defining dishes of Palermo and Sicilian cucina povera cooking. The name refers to the beccafico bird (a warbler), whose plump silhouette the stuffed and rolled sardines are said to resemble. The dish combines Norman-Arab sweet-and-savoury cooking with the abundant sardines of the Sicilian coast. The stuffing of breadcrumbs, pine nuts, raisins, and citrus reflects the Arab-influenced agrodolce tradition of Sicilian cooking. Pino Correnti, Il libro d'oro della cucina e dei vini di Sicilia (1976, Mursia), and Mary Taylor Simeti, Pomp and Sustenance: Twenty-Five Centuries of Sicilian Food (1989, Knopf), both document sarde a beccafico as a central Palermitan dish, noting its origins in the cucina baronale (aristocratic kitchen) filtered down into the popular tradition.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Stuff and roll the sardines up to 2 hours ahead and refrigerate, ready to bake.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sardines with the backbone and head removed so the fish opens flat like a book. A fishmonger will do this on request. The sardine is kept in one piece with the two fillets attached at the belly: it is then rolled around the stuffing from the head end toward the tail.

The Italian sweet-and-sour tradition, particularly prominent in Sicilian cooking. In sarde a beccafico it is expressed by the raisins and pine nuts in the stuffing alongside the breadcrumbs and savoury anchovies.

content.text: Sarde a beccafico is a study in Sicilian
(sweet-and-savoury) cooking. Breadcrumbs toasted in olive oil, pine nuts, raisins, anchovy, and orange zest go inside a
fresh sardine. The sardine is rolled up, stood upright in a baking dish, and baked until golden. The raisins give sweetness, the anchovy gives salt, and the breadcrumbs give body and texture.

Ask the fishmonger to butterfly the sardines: remove the head, slit along the belly, open flat, and remove the backbone, leaving the two fillets attached at the tail. If only whole sardines are available, do this at home with a sharp flexible knife.

items.prepNote: about 12 to 16 sardines, butterflied by the fishmonger

content.text: Warm {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a frying pan over a medium heat. Add {{breadcrumbs-coarse}} of breadcrumbs and stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and toasted. Remove and cool slightly. Combine with {{pine-nuts}} of pine nuts, {{raisins}} of raisins, {{anchovy-fillets}} of finely chopped anchovies, {{parsley-flat}} of parsley, the orange zest, and a little salt. Taste and adjust.
Heat the oven to 190°C fan (210°C conventional). Oil a baking dish large enough to hold the sardines standing upright.

Open each butterflied sardine skin-side down. Place a teaspoon of filling at the head end. Roll the sardine from head to tail into a tight cylinder. Stand it upright in the baking dish with the tail fin pointing up. Place a bay leaf between each sardine.

Drizzle {{orange-juice}} of orange juice and 2 tablespoons of olive oil over the sardines. Scatter any remaining filling over the top. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes until the sardines are cooked through and the tops are golden.

items.cause: Not packed tightly enough in the dish
items.fix: Pack the sardines upright so they support each other. If the dish is too large, use a smaller one or fill gaps with additional bay leaves.

items.cause: Too much filling, or sardines not rolled tightly enough
items.fix: Use a teaspoon of filling per sardine. Roll firmly from the head end and pack tightly into the dish before baking.

content.text: Sarde a beccafico is the unofficial dish of Palermo. It appears in the Vucciria and Ballarò markets, in neighbourhood restaurants across the city, and on family tables every Sunday. The flavours, sweet, salty, and herbal together, are pure Arab-Norman Sicily: the legacy of centuries of different peoples cooking with the same ingredients. It began as a way of making sardines go further with a cheap stuffing. It is now one of the finest expressions of Sicilian cooking.
